newsitem.title: USA: PepsiCo turns to new fronts in cola war.
newsitem.headline: PepsiCo turns to new fronts in cola war.

text.p: Stung by setbacks in the global cola wars, PepsiCo is retrenching from losing markets and planning drives in countries where it thinks it can establish a foothold.

In detailing a major restructuring, PepsiCo executives on Friday said they would pull back from costly efforts to gain market share in countries such as Brazil, where the world's biggest soft drink company, Coca-Cola Co dominates.
Industry analysts praised the strategy but said it could be a year before it shows results.

"They've been pouring money into different parts of the world, and when they stop pouring it indiscriminately there's the opportunity for margins and returns to improve," Schroder Wertheim analyst Caroline Levy said.
In the meantime, PepsiCo "will be a very painful stock to own," she added.

PepsiCo plans to turn its attention to relatively untapped markets including China, India and the former Soviet Union that hold the best prospects for future soft-drink growth, PepsiCo chief executive Roger Enrico said in a telephone conference.
"We can compete toe-to-toe where consumer loyalty is not highly established, or certainly where its established in our favor," he said.

Pepsi has been stung by setbacks in its worldwide war with Coke in places including Brazil and South Africa, where large investments have not resulted in major inroads against its arch rival, analysts said. In August, Pepsi's former bottler in Venezuela defected to Coke.
"There are certain markets where consumers have a lot of brand loyalty," Enrico said.
"And no matter how much you're willing to invest, you just can't make big gains fast against a well-established market leader," he added.
The new strategy of cutting costs by $100 million a year and focusing its international soft-drink sales strategy may pay off, analysts said. But the payoff may not be seen until 1998, they said.

"It's a matter of giving their international business more discipline and really focusing on profit growth and not necessarily market share, " said Mitchell Pinheiro of Janney Montgomery Scott. "I think they can do it."
Shares in PepsiCo were off 1-3/4 to 28-1/2 Friday afternoon. Coca-Cola dipped 1/2 to 51.
International sales made up about a third of Pepsi's 1995 total beverage sales of $10.5 billion. But foreign markets are where the biggest opportunities for growth lie, analysts said.

Late Thursday, PepsiCo unveiled a major restructuring that included over $500 million in charges. Pepsi said it will take steps needed to reduce its exposure to Buenos Aires Embotelladora SA, its Argentina-based bottler that reported a $251 million loss for the latest quarter and has been struggling to refinance about $650 million in debt.

It said it will accelerate the sale of its Pizza Hut and Taco Bell restaurants to franchisees, and include Kentucky Fried Chicken outlets in the program starting next year. It will also sell its Hot 'n Now hamburger restaurants.
Analysts said they also expected Pepsi to unload its casual dining business that includes California Pizza Kitchen, East Side Marios's and Chevy's.
"I think they're going to look around and see what the can get" for them, Wheat First Butcher Singer's John Maxwell said.

PepsiCo said its third quarter earnings would be $0.30 below the same period last year, when it earned $0.39. On Friday the company said its 1997 earnings would likely be about $0.10 below current forecasts.
Analysts' mean forcast for PepsiCo's 1997 earnings is for $1.62 a share.
Levy, meanwhile, held up Russia as an example that Coca-Cola, spending aggressively internationally, will not roll over and allow Pepsi to easily gain market share around the globe.
"Pepsi outsold them 10 to one in Russia five years ago, and Coke is now the number one selling brand" there, she said.
--New York Newsdesk, 212-859-1733
